A fresh month of home track action brought the best of the best to Central Ontario on Saturday, August 1st as a 50-lap SwitchTire Mini Stock shootout main event highlighted the night’s program at Peterborough Speedway. Current point leader Bailey Jacobs and Dan Archibald brought the Super Stock starting field from the staging area for a 25-lap feature tilt. Jacobs grabbed the lead from the drop of the green flag, but he had a quartet of heavy hitters battling for position behind him. The Warsaw, ON-based No. 60 machine broke away from the pack and logged another solid performance to take the win in the caution-free headliner. Herb Walters and Paul Boundy followed the two-time track champion under the checkered flag. [caption id="attachment_54762" align="alignnone" width="900"] Current point leader and two-time track champion Bailey Jacobs (No. 60) picked-up the Super Stock headline event win on Saturday, August 1st at Peterborough Speedway. CREDIT: Jessica Blair – Follow Me Photography[/caption] Shawn Murray and Isaiah Switzer were in control of the Trent Lakes Complete Plumbing Renegade Truck starting grid, with 20 laps on the table. Murray took the initial race lead, with Scott Jacobs, Howie Crowe and James Townsend – in the Gordon Racing No. 52 truck – close behind. Murray was turning in a strong run, while Crowe and Townsend had their own battle, taking turns in the runner-up position before the halfway mark. Townsend – who's been solid in every main event on his 2026 schedule – took the lead with a dozen laps on the scoreboard and held on for another win. Murray, Crowe, Jacobs and Switzer completed the top-five in the night’s second caution-free main event. [caption id="attachment_54763" align="alignnone" width="900"] James Townsend (No. 52) claimed the Trent Lakes Complete Plumbing Renegade Truck feature event win on Saturday, August 1st at Peterborough Speedway. CREDIT: Jessica Blair – Follow Me Photography[/caption] Nadeau’s Collision Service Junior Late Model action came to the line with a 15-lap or 20-minute agenda, led by Kaiden Beatty and Dylan Ephgrave on the front row. The lead duo broke away at the drop of the green flag and started putting slower traffic a lap down with just over a handful of circuits complete. With the field of talented young racers searching high and low for an advantage, Beatty pushed his No. 86k to its limits and had a commanding lead over his closest rival. On a night where caution-free features were the rule instead of the exception, Beatty took the checkered flag over Brody Coates, Owen Ephgrave, Brayden Cappuccitti and Troy Purvis. In post-race inspection, Beatty was found to have used an illegal track width and was disqualified. Coates was credited with the win, with Lyla Sikma moved into the top-five. With a stellar field of nearly 25 starters in tow, Shawn Dearmer and Alexis Melhuish brought the Battlefield Equipment Rental Bone Stock line-up to the Great Canadian RV green flag. Former track champion Shawn Solomon took the early lead as the pack caught the tail end of the field with nearly 10 of the 20-lap race distance complete. With the No. 19 machine holding the hot hand, the lead group formed an attack on the outside line. Kyle Novis moved into the runner-up spot with 13 laps on the scoreboard and had reigning track champion Alex Dallaire and 2025 rookie of the year Jacob Stavropoulos looking for a way to the front. Solomon led the pack to the checkered flag. Novis, Dallaire, Stavropoulos and Steve Oakes completed the top-five. In post-race inspection, the No. 19 of Shawn Solomon was discovered to have rear tires not in line with the front tires and was disqualified. Kyle Novis was declared the race winner. [caption id="attachment_54764" align="alignnone" width="900"] After post-race issues for the first car across the line, Kyle Novis (No. 21) was awarded the Battlefield Equipment Rental Bone Stock win on Saturday, August 1st at Peterborough Speedway. CREDIT: Jessica Blair – Follow Me Photography[/caption] Action wrapped up with a 50-lap Shootout for the SwitchTire Mini Stocks that started with Rob Crick and Cory Horne on the front row. Tiffany Vandebelt was the early race leader when the night’s first feature-race caution flag waved for a turn two incident, with three laps complete. James Townsend charged to third and then the runner-up spot just after the restart, with the leaders putting some backmarkers a lap down with 15 laps on the scoreboard. The pilot of the No. 14 ride took the lead and survived a late-race yellow flag to keep his 2026 Peterborough Speedway unbeaten streak alive. Rob Crick, point leader John Lavalle, Kyle Abbott and Vandebelt were next across the line. Townsend’s Mini Stock Shootout win resulted in a $550 bank deposit. The Peterborough Speedway winner’s share was $350, with another $150 from Fenney Call Photography and a $50 halfway leader bonus from Clarke Motorsports Communications. Coltin Everingham and Herb Walters locked-up main event starting positions with Super Stock preliminary round checkered flags. James Townsend and Shawn Murray shared the Renegade Truck heat race wins. Junior Late Model qualifiers went to Brayden Cappuccitti and Brody Coates. A trio of Bone Stock heat races were split between Jacob Stavropoulos, Kyle Novis and Alex Dallaire. Dave Bragg and James Townsend scored Mini Stock qualifiers. All finishing positions are unofficial until verified by scoring review and post-race inspection. Bullring Bullet Points:
  • James Townsend took another turn in the Gordon Racing No. 52 Renegade Truck. Mechanical issues discovered after the pre-race practice session sidelined the No. 37 pick-up of Stacy Switzer.
  • The No. 01 Bone Stock ride was piloted by Shannon Cappuccitti.
  • It was a tough night for the No. 83 Mini Stock and driver Cameron McGlashan. After experiencing oil pressure issues in his own car, he picked-up a ride in a car Coltin Everingham had been slated to run. That car also suffered a mechanical failure and was finished for the night.
  • 2023 track champion and 2026 feature winner Miles Tyson was unable to start the night’s Super Stock main event.
  • ’The Dentman’ Dave Watchorn made the tow from North Gower with his vintage Toyota to run the 50-lap Mini Stock Shootout.
  • Former track champion and Ontario Modifieds Racing Series competitor Willow Barberstock made her first start of the year. Unfortunately, it was a short night as mechanical issues sidelined her No. 62 effort early in the Bone Stock feature.
  • Dan Demers of nearby Cavan continued a streak of making at least one start a year by taking the Mini Stock Shootout green flag.
  • The night’s Kinsmen 50/50 draw prize of $602.50 went home with Barb Mooy.
Next on the weekly agenda will be the home track Bone Stock and Late Model divisions, along with the Trailers Plus Ontario Legend Cars and KOD Disposal Ontario Bandoleros. The Ontario Sportsman Series will also be on hand for the Silver Wheel 100 presented by AF Automotive Fluids ‘A’ main, with Kid’s Barrel Races as the intermission feature. Stay on top of the latest track news and schedule information by following www.peterboroughspeedway.com or the venue’s social media platforms and pages.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text: 2 America Square, an office block leased by a Virgin Islands-based company, is at the centre of the court case. Photograph: Brian Anthony/Alamy View image in fullscreen 2 America Square, an office block leased by a Virgin Islands-based company, is at the centre of the court case. Photograph: Brian Anthony/Alamy Financial sector The London office, the empty boxes and the £1bn tax loophole Exclusive: How a court case over an unoccupied office block could end a widely used tax avoidance scheme Nick Sommerlad Mon 31 Aug 2026 08.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 08.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google From the outside, the seven-storey building at 2 America Square looks like any other office block in the heart of London’s financial district. Located about half a mile from Tower Bridge, one might expect it to be a hive of commercial activity, teeming with employees holding important meetings. However, much of the property is home not to staff vying for their next bonus, but to stacks of nondescript black boxes arranged in neat lines. The building, leased by a Virgin Islands-based company called 48th Street Holdings Ltd, has found itself at the centre of a court case that has finally signalled the end of a tax avoidance scheme believed to have cost local authorities more than £1bn. For almost two decades, companies in England have been exploiting a legal loophole to avoid paying business rates on unoccupied commercial buildings. The controversial practice dates back to 2008, when the last Labour government changed business rates rules. This meant occupiers of vacant buildings no longer qualified for a 50% discount on the levy. View image in fullscreen Boxes such as these enabled companies to claim three-month rate holidays on unoccupied properties. Photograph: City of London Corporation However, they were entitled to claim a three-month rate holiday at the end of each tenancy – and the “box shifting” scheme was born. With commercial property owners facing higher bills, a lucrative “rate mitigation” industry emerged. Historically, this typically involved boxes being moved into the empty space at the end of the three months and back out after just six weeks. The building then became unoccupied again and the clock was reset, allowing the owner to claim another three-month rate-free period. This cycle continued, designed to cut the rates owed by up to 67%, until a new long-term tenant could be found. It has been costing one London council an estimated £35m a year since the pandemic, when the number of claims for empty property relief doubled. However, last month a landmark ruling by three court of appeal judges looks to have sounded the death knell for box shifting. They ruled that the scheme “cannot amount to beneficial occupation”. locator map The case was brought by the City of London Corporation against 48th Street Holding Ltd and a second company, Principled Offsite Logistics Ltd (POLL), which provides “rate mitigation” services. 48th Street paid £27.6m for a lease on the office block in 2019 before it brought in POLL to save £111,475.30 in rates across a series of three-month periods in 2022 and 2023. POLL describes itself as “the largest and most reliable” provider of “empty business rates mitigation” in the UK and is jointly owned by a Labour councillor from North Hertfordshire. It claimed by 2021 to have already saved its clients “£500m” in rates and that “every council in the UK now totally recognises Principled as being robust in every way”. That bold claim followed a significant high court win in 2018, when POLL defeated a challenge from Trafford council. The judge in that case accepted that “the purpose of the occupation is not to store goods; it is, so to speak, to plant the occupier’s flag” and that “the motive … is rates avoidance for the landlord”, but added “the morality of that is neither here nor there”. When the case against POLL and 48th Street came before the high court last year, Charles Bagot KC, sitting as a deputy high court judge, also ruled against the City of London. “I agree with POLL that if legislation produces clear tramlines and someone organises themselves to fall within them, then it is not for the court to get involved in moral judgments,” he said. “If the government does not like the position, it can amend it.” He concluded that “the RMS [rate mitigation scheme] is effective”. However, last month the court of appeal overturned that decision, with Lady Justice Falk ruling: “In my judgment, ‘occupation’ for, in effect, the sake of it, and which has no use, value or benefit other than rate saving, does not amount to occupation for the purpose of the statutory scheme.” A City of London Corporation spokesperson said: “We welcome the court of appeal’s decision, which represents a significant victory for local authorities across England. “This landmark ruling closes one of the most widely used tax avoidance schemes in the country and helps safeguard revenues that support essential public services. “We are proud that the City of London Corporation has led the way nationally in pursuing this case. “For more than a decade, councils across the country have seen hundreds of millions of pounds of public revenue lost through artificial business rates avoidance schemes and we believe the decision restores fairness, protects money that funds vital local services, and provides greater certainty for councils, ratepayers and property owners alike.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines UK Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning after newsletter promotion A government spokesperson said: “We recognise concerns about the misuse of Empty Property Relief, which exists to support genuine property owners between tenants. “Business rates avoidance is unacceptable and we are taking the necessary action to address this, and make sure that businesses are paying the tax they owe.” It is unclear what action the government is planning, but there are calls for a general anti-avoidance rule to control the rate mitigation industry. POLL is not the only business offering box shifting. The same scheme was even used by Public Health England at its future headquarters in Harlow in 2018. The resulting £2.5m dispute with Harlow district council ended up in the high court, where PHE won. It remains to be seen how councils and their rate mitigation opponents will respond. One rating expert said that the total cost to councils of box shifting could have topped £1.5bn, and some of that money should now be reclaimed as a deterrent. Under the terms of POLL’s contracts with clients, its success fees are refundable in the event the scheme fails. The latest accounts show it has just over £500,000 in net assets. POLL did not respond to a request for comment and its website went down this week, replaced with a message which read: “This account has been suspended”. The company’s founder, Steven Dawson, died in 2024 and the POLL was acquired in a management buyout by two of its own executives. One of them is a Labour councillor, Sarah Lucas , who, according to her LinkedIn profile, has been POLL’s director of finance since 2018. View image in fullscreen The boxes are a key element of a ‘rate mitigation’ scheme estimated to have cost local authorities over £1bn. Photograph: City of London Corporation Lucas was elected to North Hertfordshire council in 2024, two months after she took 50% ownership of POLL, and she serves as vice-chair of the council’s finance, audit and risk committee. The Guardian understands that POLL’s application for permission to appeal to the supreme court was refused by the court of appeal this week but an option remains for it to apply to the supreme court directly. The rules on empty property relief changed in 2024 and buildings now need to be occupied for 13 weeks instead of six in order for the three-month holiday to apply. According to one recent judgment, this makes box shifting schemes “less attractive but still effective”. There are still a range of variants of rates mitigation on offer. One involves placing Bluetooth boxes in the offices to broadcast adverts. Another uses charitable exhibitions to claim not only empty property relief but also the extra rates relief available for charities. Some schemes install snail or mushroom farms to claim agricultural reliefs, while others involve opening faith rooms to cut rates. https://bnn-news.com/following-widesprea.text: Baltics Social Politics Money Interviews Opinions In Focus World Leisure Advertising Baltics Social Politics Money Interviews Opinions In Focus World Leisure Advertising Home Baltics Latvia Latvia Politics Social Following widespread public reaction, ministry withdraws draft on state of emergency in Latvia’s border region LETA August 27, 2026 Facebook Twitter Photo: Ivars Soikāns/LETA The Ministry of Climate and Energy (KEM) has withdrawn the draft order submitted for inter-agency approval on Wednesday, the 26th of August, which envisaged declaring a state of emergency in the healthcare, energy supply and water management sectors in Latvia’s eastern border region, according to information published on the Draft Legal Acts (TAP) portal. KEM representatives told the LETA news agency that, in light of discussions in the public domain and what the ministry considers to be some inaccurate interpretations of the document’s substance and purpose, the document is currently no longer publicly available on the TAP portal. To reduce the risk of further communication problems and misinterpretation, the ministry also plans to clarify the title of the document. At the same time, the information provided by KEM does not indicate that the initiative itself or the draft order has been abandoned. The ministry is continuing work on a temporary legal solution, while the next step will be to develop permanent regulations governing the provision of critical services during an aerial threat over the long term. KEM also stated that it initiated the drafting of the relevant Cabinet of Ministers order on the basis of a government instruction requiring all ministries, where necessary, to submit proposals to the Ministry of Justice by the 30th of September this year for the legal framework needed in their respective sectors to ensure continuity of operations in the event of threats to Latvia’s airspace. The ministries were instructed to clearly define the objective or problem, propose a conceptual solution for achieving that objective or addressing the problem, and explain why the issue cannot be resolved under the existing legislation governing their respective sectors. As previously reported, KEM had prepared and submitted for inter-agency approval a draft order proposing that a state of emergency be declared until the 1st of December this year in the healthcare, energy supply and water management sectors in Latvia’s eastern border region. The proposal was justified by the threat of an escalation in Russia’s military activities and the need to address potential threats to Latvia’s airspace. The proposed state of emergency would have applied to the municipalities of Alūksne, Augšdaugava, Balvi, Daugavpils, Krāslava, Līvāni, Ludza, Preiļi and Rēzekne, as well as the cities of Daugavpils and Rēzekne. KEM explained that unmanned aerial vehicles and other unidentified objects are being detected with increasing frequency in Latvian airspace or near the country’s border, potentially posing a threat to public safety, human health and the operation of critical infrastructure. The draft order provided for temporary exemptions from working-time and overtime regulations, additional remuneration and employee protection measures to ensure the continuity of critical services during an aerial threat. Minister of Climate and Energy Jānis Vitenbergs (National Alliance) explained on Thursday that the draft order concerning a state of emergency in Latvia’s border region was not a signal of an imminent invasion, but rather a preventive measure intended to ensure the continuity of critical services in the event of an aerial threat. KEM stressed that the draft order, entitled “On Declaring a State of Emergency in Latvia’s Eastern Border Region,” did not itself provide for the immediate declaration of a state of emergency, but instead set out measures to be taken if such a state of emergency were declared. Photograph: Hampshire Constabulary/PA View image in fullscreen CCTV images issued by police of six men they would like to speak to after scenes of violent disorder at Eastney Marina. Photograph: Hampshire Constabulary/PA Portsmouth Police release images of six men sought after violent disorder in Portsmouth Hampshire and Isle of Wight force says it wants to speak to men in connection with anti-migrant unrest that left seven officers injured Nadia Khomami Sun 13 Sep 2026 11.45 EDT Last modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 11.58 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Police have released images of six men they would like to speak to after violent disorder in Portsmouth last week that left seven officers injured. About 200 people gathered at Eastney Marina on Sunday night after a small boat carrying asylum seekers arrived on the south coast having crossed the Channel. The activists dispersed the following day in the early hours. Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary said seven police officers were injured and treated at the scene, while vehicles belonging to the Coastguard and Border Force were damaged. The force said it reviewed “hundreds of hours’ worth” of footage from the disorder and released images of six men it believes “can assist our investigation”. The first person charged in connection with the demonstration in the city appeared in court on Saturday morning. Del Leon Somerville, 42, from Paulsgrove, Portsmouth, appeared at the city’s magistrates court charged with violent disorder and assaulting a police constable. A 16-year-old boy from Waterlooville was also arrested on suspicion of violent disorder in connection with last Sunday’s events. He has been released on bail until 12 December. Anti-immigration activists returned to the streets of Portsmouth on Saturday afternoon, where they faced counter-protests from anti-racism groups. Tony Rowlinson, assistant chief constable, said the scenes at Eastney Marina had gone beyond peaceful protest. “Violence and criminal damage have no part in peaceful protest,” he said. “Clearly events on Sunday evening were not peaceful protest, rather violent public disorder.” Rowlinson said officers had worked to protect people in the area and warned that police would pursue those responsible after reviewing footage. “The reality of public order policing is that arrests at the time are not always possible, especially where evidence may need to be reviewed to clearly identify who is responsible for offences,” he said. He added that none of the seven injured officers had been seriously hurt, but said they “did not deserve to be assaulted” while policing the demonstration. Police also said they were investigating online threats and abuse directed at officers and staff from partner agencies after the disorder. The force has appealed to anyone who recognises the six men to contact police on 101 or report information online, quoting reference 44260435943. Rowlinson said: “If you break the law we will take action against you and where it is feasible to do so seek a prosecution.” Explore more on these topics Portsmouth Protest Refugees Immigration and asylum Far right news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland
